questions.question: What does a VPN create between your device and its server?
options: A backup copy of your files
An encrypted tunnel that hides your traffic from ISPs, admins, and hackers
questions.explanation: Tumhare device aur VPN server ke beech encrypted tunnel — ISP, network admin, hackers koi nahi dekh sakta tum kya browse kar rahe ho.

questions.question: Which analogy does the guide use to describe a VPN?
options: An opaque armored tube versus a glass tunnel that everyone can see through
questions.explanation: Normal internet = glass tunnel — sab dekh sakte hain. VPN = opaque armored tube — bahar se kuch nazar nahi.

questions.question: What warning does the guide give about free VPN services?
options: They are illegal in every country
They are always faster than paid VPNs
They cannot be used on mobile devices
questions.explanation: Free VPNs se beware — they sell your data. Privacy protect karne ke naam pe khud data bech sakte hain.

questions.question: You connect to a coffee shop's public WiFi while using a VPN, and even someone monitoring the WiFi network cannot see which websites you're visiting. What is enabling this protection?
questions.explanation: VPN encrypted tunnel banaata hai — public WiFi pe safety ke liye ek prime use case hai.

questions.question: What IP address does a website see when you're browsing through a VPN?
options: Your actual home IP address, unchanged
The VPN server's IP address, not your own
questions.explanation: Tumhara IP bhi VPN server ka IP dikhta hai — yeh regional content access aur privacy ke liye use hota hai.

questions.question: What does network segmentation do?
options: Combines multiple small networks into one large network
Encrypts all data on a single server
Divides a large network into smaller isolated segments to contain damage
Blocks all outbound internet traffic entirely
questions.explanation: Ek bada network ko smaller segments mein divide karna (VLANs, subnets) — finance network se developer network alag.

questions.question: What specific attack behavior does network segmentation help prevent?
options: Lateral movement — an attacker moving freely across the whole network after compromising one machine
questions.explanation: Lateral movement prevent karta hai — attacker ek machine compromise kare par poore network mein freely nahi ghoom sakta.

questions.question: A worm compromises one workstation in the marketing department, but is unable to spread into the finance department's systems because they sit on a completely separate network segment. What prevented the spread?
questions.explanation: Ek zone compromise ho to doosre safe rahein — yeh network segmentation ka core benefit hai, jaise Colonial Pipeline worm ko bhi is se roka ja sakta tha.

questions.question: Which real-world incident does the guide say could have been contained better with proper network segmentation?
questions.explanation: Colonial Pipeline worm bhi segmentation se rok sakte the — guide is example ko specifically mention karti hai.

questions.question: Which technical tools does the guide mention for implementing network segmentation?
questions.explanation: Ek bada network ko smaller segments mein divide karna (VLANs, subnets) — yeh technical implementation ka tareeka hai.

questions.question: What happens during DNS poisoning?
options: Fake records get injected into a DNS server's cache, redirecting users to the wrong IP
A user's browser history gets deleted
All DNS servers worldwide go offline simultaneously
A DNS server is physically destroyed
questions.explanation: DNS server ki cache mein fake records inject karna — 'google.com = galat IP' record return karta hai, user attacker site pe pahunch jaata hai.

questions.question: How does the guide describe what DNS itself is, before explaining poisoning?
options: A type of encrypted messaging protocol
The 'phone book' of the internet, translating domain names into IP addresses
questions.explanation: Phone book of internet — 'google.com' → '142.250.195.46' translate karta hai. DNS poisoning is phonebook mein galat entries daalna hai.

questions.question: A user types 'google.com' correctly into their browser, but ends up on a fake malicious website instead. Which attack likely caused this, assuming their own device isn't infected?
questions.explanation: DNS poisoning se galat IP wapas milta hai even though URL sahi type kiya gaya — user ko pata bhi nahi chalta ki fake site pe pahunch gaya.

questions.question: What does a poisoned DNS cache record for a legitimate domain like 'google.com' actually contain?
options: The user's own personal IP address
The correct IP address, but encrypted differently
An incorrect IP address controlled by the attacker
questions.explanation: 'google.com = 1.2.3.4' — yeh galat IP hai par DNS ye record return karta hai jab poisoning ho chuki ho.

questions.question: DNS poisoning is essentially an attack on which core internet function?
options: Domain name to IP address translation
questions.explanation: DNS ka core function domain name ko IP address mein translate karna hai — poisoning isi function ko corrupt karta hai.

questions.question: What is the primary security benefit of NAT (Network Address Translation)?
options: It encrypts all internet traffic automatically
Internal devices' private IPs are hidden from the internet, so they can't be accessed directly
It blocks all malware regardless of source
questions.explanation: Router andar private IPs maintain karta hai, internet se direct access nahi hota internal devices ko — security benefit.

questions.question: In a typical home network, what does the outside internet see?
options: Only the phone's IP, never the laptop's
Every individual device's private IP address
Only the router's single public IP address
Nothing at all, the network is invisible
questions.explanation: Router: 103.45.67.89 — public IP. Internet pe sirf router ka IP dikhta hai, andar ke devices ke private IPs hidden rehte hain.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a private IP address, as shown in the guide's home network example?
questions.explanation: Phone: 192.168.1.5, Laptop: 192.168.1.6 — yeh private IPs hain, sirf ghar ke network ke andar valid.

questions.question: An attacker scanning the internet cannot directly find or connect to your home laptop's private IP address, even though they can see your router's public IP. What is providing this protection?
questions.explanation: NAT internal devices ko internet se direct access se protect karta hai, sirf router ka public IP visible hota hai.

questions.question: What does NAT stand for?
questions.explanation: NAT = Network Address Translation — private IPs hide karna internet se, security ka ek natural side-benefit.

questions.question: What does SDN (Software Defined Networking) enable compared to traditional networks?
options: Removing the need for any network security at all
Physically rewiring the network every time a policy changes
Centralized, software-based control of the network instead of manual hardware configuration
questions.explanation: Traditional networks mein hardware configure karo manually. SDN mein software se network control hota hai centrally.

questions.question: What security advantage does SDN offer when a threat is detected?
options: It permanently deletes all network logs
It requires a technician to physically unplug a cable
It disables the internet for the entire company
The SDN controller can automatically isolate the affected network segment
questions.explanation: Threat detect hote hi, SDN controller automatically affected segment isolate kar sakta hai — faster response to threats.

questions.question: Which environments does the guide say typically rely on SDN-like architecture?
questions.explanation: Cloud networks aise hi work karte hain — micro-segmentation easily implement, SDN-based architecture common hai.

questions.question: As soon as a security tool flags anomalous traffic, the network automatically reconfigures itself in seconds to isolate the affected segment, without any human manually reconfiguring hardware. What technology enables this rapid response?
questions.explanation: SDN security policies dynamically apply ho sakti hain — automated, fast response jo traditional hardware configuration se possible nahi tha.

questions.question: What does SDN make easier to implement, according to the guide?
questions.explanation: Micro-segmentation easily implement — SDN ki flexibility isse possible banati hai.

questions.question: What does a CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker) primarily monitor?
options: What data employees send to cloud apps and detect unauthorized ('shadow IT') app usage
Physical access to the server room
questions.explanation: Employees cloud apps (Google Drive, Dropbox, Salesforce) use karte hain — CASB monitor karta hai kya data cloud pe ja raha hai.

questions.question: What is 'shadow IT', which a CASB helps detect?
options: A backup server hidden in a data center
A hacking group operating in the dark web
Unauthorized apps or cloud services being used without IT department approval
questions.explanation: Unauthorized apps ka use ('shadow IT') detect karta hai — jab employees bina approval ke apne cloud tools use karte hain.

questions.question: An employee uploads a confidential company document to their personal Dropbox account, and a security tool immediately flags and alerts the security team. Which tool caught this?
questions.explanation: Employee ne confidential doc Dropbox personal pe upload kiya, CASB detect karta hai — alert ya block. DLP + cloud = CASB.

questions.question: How does the guide describe CASB in relation to DLP?
options: CASB replaces the need for any encryption
CASB has nothing to do with DLP
CASB is essentially DLP combined with cloud visibility
CASB is only for physical security
questions.explanation: DLP + cloud = CASB — guide explicitly is combination ko describe karti hai.

questions.question: Which of these apps would a CASB typically monitor employee usage of?
options: Only the company's physical badge system
questions.explanation: Employees cloud apps (Google Drive, Dropbox, Salesforce) use karte hain — CASB inhi apps pe data flow monitor karta hai.

questions.question: What is the Internet of Things (IoT)?
options: Internet-connected physical devices like smart bulbs, cameras, and thermostats
questions.explanation: Smart devices jo internet se connected hain — smart bulbs, cameras, fridges, thermostats, wearables, industrial sensors, medical devices.

questions.question: How many IoT devices are expected globally by 2030, according to the guide?
questions.explanation: 2030 tak 75 billion+ IoT devices expected — har device ek potential entry point banta hai.

questions.question: What common security problem does the guide highlight about most IoT devices?
options: They often have weak passwords, outdated firmware, and no security updates
They cannot connect to the internet at all
They are only used by governments
They are always more secure than laptops
questions.explanation: Most IoT devices have terrible security — no updates, weak passwords, old firmware — isliye har device ek potential entry point banta hai.

questions.question: A smart doorbell, a smart thermostat, and a smart TV in your house all still have their default factory passwords set. What does this collectively represent?
options: An expanded attack surface due to poor IoT security practices
A guaranteed DDoS attack within 24 hours
No risk at all since they're just household appliances
questions.explanation: Default passwords change na karna common IoT mistake hai — har unsecured device ek potential entry point ban jaata hai attackers ke liye.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of an IoT device, according to the guide's list?
questions.explanation: Smart bulbs, cameras, fridges, thermostats, wearables, industrial sensors, medical devices — sab IoT devices hain.

questions.question: Why does the guide describe securing IoT devices as especially difficult?
options: Because IoT devices don't connect to the internet at all
Because IoT devices are always encrypted by default
Because IoT devices have unlimited processing power
Limited processing power, no screen for setup, and vendors rarely issue updates
questions.explanation: Limited processing power (can't run complex security), no screen/keyboard for setup, vendors update nahi karte, users default passwords change nahi karte.

questions.question: In the 2017 casino hack, attackers used a smart fish tank thermometer to exfiltrate how much data from the casino's high-roller database?
questions.explanation: Casino ka smart fish tank thermometer hack hua — attackers ne isse network access liya aur casino's high-roller database exfiltrate ki, 10GB data.

questions.question: Which of these is a recommended best practice for IoT security, according to the guide?
options: Keep IoT devices on a separate network/VLAN from critical systems
Connect every IoT device directly to the main corporate network
Always keep default passwords unchanged for compatibility
Never update IoT device firmware, to avoid breaking it
questions.explanation: Default passwords change karo, separate network/VLAN pe rakho IoT devices, firmware update karo, unnecessary features disable karo, network monitoring rakho.

questions.question: A seemingly harmless smart device on a network becomes the entry point for a much larger data breach into supposedly unrelated systems. Which real-world incident does this describe?
options: The casino fish tank thermometer hack
questions.explanation: Hospital/casino hack via fish tank thermometer (2017) — exactly is scenario ko describe karta hai, ek chhota IoT device bada breach ka entry point bana.

questions.question: Why is IoT device lifecycle a security challenge, according to the guide?
options: Devices never need power and thus never need updates
Devices are replaced every month, causing config chaos
Devices are always managed by a dedicated IT team
Devices can remain in use for 10-20 years, often without ongoing security support
questions.explanation: Long lifecycle (10-20 years) — vendor support kabhi khatam ho jaata hai but device abhi bhi use ho raha hota hai, security gap create karta hai.

questions.question: What does Network Security encompass, as an umbrella term?
options: Only physical locks on server room doors
Only antivirus software installed on individual laptops
Policies, tools, and practices that protect network infrastructure from unauthorized access, misuse, and denial
questions.explanation: Policies, tools, aur practices jo network infrastructure protect karte hain — unauthorized access, misuse, modification, denial prevent karna.

questions.question: What is 'defense in depth', as described in the guide's Network Security layers?
options: Removing all layers to simplify the network
Only using antivirus and nothing else
Relying on a single very strong firewall alone
Using multiple layers (firewall, IDS, WAF, endpoint, SIEM) so that if one layer fails, another catches the threat
questions.explanation: Defense in depth — ek layer breach ho to doosri catch kare. Firewall → IDS → WAF → Endpoint → SIEM — layered approach best practice hai.

questions.question: Which of these tools is listed as a component of overall Network Security?
questions.explanation: Firewall, IDS/IPS, VPN, segmentation sab Network Security ke components hain.

questions.question: An attacker bypasses the firewall, but is then caught by the IDS, and even if that failed too, the WAF would have blocked the web-layer attack anyway. What security philosophy is being demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Ek layer breach ho to doosri catch kare — yeh defense in depth ka core idea hai, multiple layers overlapping protection dete hain.

questions.question: Which order does the guide list as a typical layered defense-in-depth stack?
questions.explanation: Firewall → IDS → WAF → Endpoint → SIEM — layered approach best practice hai jo guide mein specifically likha gaya hai.

questions.question: What is a 'threat actor'?
options: Anyone who carries out a cyberattack, regardless of their motivation or skill level
Only a piece of malicious software
Only a government employee working in cybersecurity
questions.explanation: Koi bhi jo cyberattack kare — multiple types: nation-state, cybercriminals, hacktivists, insider threats, script kiddies.

questions.question: Which threat actor type is primarily motivated by political causes?
questions.explanation: Hacktivists: Political (Anonymous) — cybercriminals financial motivation rakhte hain, nation-state government-backed hote hain.

questions.question: Why does knowing the type of threat actor matter for defense, according to the guide?
options: It reveals their likely motivation and resources, helping tailor defenses accordingly
It has no practical impact on defense strategy at all
It determines which color the security badge should be
It only matters for legal prosecution, not security
questions.explanation: Threat actor type se pata chalta hai motivation kya hai, resources kitne hain — nation-state actors ka zero-day budget ≠ script kiddie ka free tools.

questions.question: A government-backed group like Russia's APT28 launches a highly sophisticated, well-funded, multi-year campaign against a target. Which threat actor category does this represent?
questions.explanation: Nation-State: government-backed (Russia APT28, China APT40) — highly resourced aur sophisticated compared to other threat actor types.

questions.question: Which threat actor type does the guide describe as motivated purely by financial gain?
questions.explanation: Cybercriminals: Financial motivation — yeh unhe hacktivists (political) ya nation-state (geopolitical) se alag karta hai.
